strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: producing reusable, high-resolution remote-sensing representations from multi-temporal Sentinel-1/Sentinel-2 data. The proposed “model-as-data” release of annual 10 m global embeddings would be practically valuable if made available as claimed.

The system is technically plausible and described with meaningful implementation detail: dual modality-specific temporal Transformer encoders, day-of-year conditioning, sparse temporal sampling, Barlow Twins-style redundancy reduction with mix-up, global shuffling over about 0.8B d-pixels from 3,012 MGRS tiles, and concrete training hyperparameters.

The evaluation spans several relevant EO applications, including crop classification, canopy height, above-ground biomass, burned area analysis, and voluntary carbon-market stocking indices. The strongest evidence appears in crop classification and biomass, where TESSERA shows clear gains over PRESTO/SpectralGPT-style baselines, especially in low-label regimes.

The representation is compact at inference time, using a 128-dimensional pixel embedding despite a large training-time projector. This is appealing for downstream users and distinguishes the contribution from models that require expensive raw-data preprocessing or end-to-end fine-tuning.
The manuscript is generally readable and communicates the motivation for preserving temporal signals and fusing SAR/optical modalities clearly.
weaknesses: The central claims of “state-of-the-art” performance are stronger than the evidence supports. Several tasks are evaluated in narrow or nonstandard ways: burned area detection is only shown via UMAP visualizations on two 15 km California regions, without quantitative classification, temporal localization, or severity metrics.

Some comparisons are potentially unfair or hard to interpret. For canopy height, TESSERA is trained locally with a 30M-parameter UNet and compared against global/static products that were not locally adapted, so the very poor R2 values of those products do not establish a foundation-model advantage. The VCM experiment fits linear conversions to only 38 field sites, which risks optimistic calibration and does not show held-out generalization.

The crop evaluation may suffer from spatial autocorrelation leakage unless train/validation/test splits are spatially disjoint. The appendix describes randomly selected subsets and held-out test data, but does not make clear that pixels from neighboring fields or the same region are separated spatially, which is material for remote-sensing classification.

Ablations are insufficient for the methodological claims. The paper does not isolate the effect of SAR versus optical fusion, temporal sampling, Barlow Twins versus alternatives, the mix-up term, projector size, embedding dimension, global shuffling, pretraining scale, or one-epoch training. Without these, it is difficult to know which ingredients drive the gains.

Reproducibility is only partially supported. The paper claims open source and public representation maps, but the manuscript provides no concrete repository, model checkpoint, data-product access path, code-release status, or exact preprocessing implementation for the custom Rust pipeline. Given the scale of the system, this materially limits independent verification.

The architecture novelty is moderate. The core design combines established components: modality-specific temporal Transformers, Barlow Twins redundancy reduction, temporal sampling augmentation, and MLP fusion. The main contribution is scale and data-product packaging rather than a clearly new learning method.

Some downstream protocols are underspecified or inconsistent across baselines, especially patch-wise segmentation where pixel-based models use constructed representation patches while patch-based foundation models use frozen encoders plus UPerNet heads. The paper does not fully establish that head capacity, input data, and training budgets are comparable.

The manuscript contains presentation and polish issues that affect confidence: placeholder text such as “REF”, typos such as “SpectralGBT”, inconsistent references to attention pooling versus GRU pooling, and missing details for the “SI” conversion functions in the visible manuscript. These are fixable but noticeable.

strengths: The problem is important and timely: learning reusable, high-resolution representations from Sentinel-1/Sentinel-2 temporal data would be valuable for many Earth observation applications.

The proposed system is practically appealing. Pixel-level annual embeddings, fusion of optical and SAR streams, and a model-as-data release could lower the barrier for downstream users if the maps, code, and weights are actually released.

The manuscript evaluates on several application domains, including crop classification, canopy height, above-ground biomass, burned area analysis, and carbon-market stocking indices. Some reported gains are substantial, especially over PRESTO on Austrian crop classification and over SpectralGPT on BioMassters under limited labels.

The method is technically plausible: separate temporal Transformer encoders for S1/S2, DOY encoding, temporal sampling augmentations, and a Barlow Twins-style objective are coherent design choices for cloud-corrupted remote-sensing time series.
Some implementation details are useful, including the number of training samples, sequence length, optimizer schedule, batch size, model size, and a description of the global shuffling pipeline.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited relative to the strength of the claims. The core method is largely an application and scaling of known components: temporal Transformers, optical/SAR fusion, sparse temporal sampling, Barlow Twins, mixup regularization, and frozen-feature downstream heads. The paper does not convincingly isolate a new algorithmic contribution beyond engineering scale and a proposed data product.

The evidence does not support the repeated state-of-the-art framing. Several comparisons are not apples-to-apples: global canopy height products are compared against a locally trained UNet on TESSERA features; BioMassters comparisons use different satellite inputs and architectures; patch-based crop segmentation uses different heads for different foundation models; and the carbon-market comparison applies fitted linear rescalings on only 38 sites.

Ablation analysis is essentially missing. The paper does not quantify the contribution of SAR versus optical data, dual encoders versus a simpler fused encoder, Barlow Twins versus other SSL objectives, mixup regularization, temporal sampling strategy, projector size, representation dimension, global shuffling, or pretraining scale. This makes the causal explanation for the gains weak.

The burned-area evaluation is only qualitative UMAP visualization on two 15 x 15 km California regions. There are no classification metrics, held-out evaluation, comparison to burned-area methods, or robustness tests, yet the text presents this as evidence of disturbance-monitoring capability.

Reproducibility is weak for a CVPR submission. The paper says the model and maps are intended to be released, but provides no actual repository, access instructions, data-product specification, preprocessing code, or exact train/validation/test splits. Downstream training details are incomplete for several tasks, especially canopy height, biomass, semantic segmentation, and the carbon-market experiment.

The manuscript has signs of incompleteness and poor polish: it contains a placeholder citation '(REF)', a typo 'SpectralGBT', 'conversation functions' instead of conversion functions, inconsistent terminology around attention pooling versus GRU pooling, and missing or vague supplementary details despite references to SI material.

The scale claims are not adequately substantiated. Producing annual global 10 m embeddings for 2017-2024 is a massive data product, but the manuscript does not report storage size, tiling format, access latency, coverage masks, uncertainty, versioning, licensing constraints, or practical validation of the released maps.

The paper overstates generality. Most strong quantitative evidence comes from a small number of geographically specific tasks: Austria crops, a 5 x 6 km Borneo canopy-height region, Finland biomass, and 38 Brazilian plots. This is not enough to conclude broadly superior global representations.

Statistical support is thin. Many figures lack confidence intervals or exact numeric tables; the manuscript often reports visual trends rather than formal tests; and there is little discussion of variance across seeds, dataset splits, geographic regions, or years.

For CVPR, the contribution reads more like a remote-sensing data/model report than a mature computer-vision methods paper. The application value could be high, but the current manuscript does not provide enough controlled evidence, methodological novelty, or reproducibility to justify acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem in remote sensing foundation models: producing reusable, temporally aware, globally available 10 m representations from Sentinel-1/2 time series. The proposed “model-as-data” framing is practically valuable, since precomputed 128-D annual embeddings could substantially lower the barrier for downstream EO users who cannot process raw satellite archives or train large models.

The technical design is sensible and well matched to the domain: separate Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 temporal encoders, DOY-aware temporal sampling, Barlow Twins-style self-supervision, and a large projector for redundancy reduction. The global shuffling strategy is a useful engineering contribution for training on spatially autocorrelated EO data at very large scale.

The empirical scope is broader than many RSFM papers. The manuscript evaluates crop classification, canopy height, biomass estimation, burned-area structure, and voluntary-carbon-market stocking indices, including low-label regimes where foundation representations are especially relevant.

Several quantitative results are compelling. TESSERA outperforms PRESTO and a Random Forest baseline on Austrian crop classification, improves over PRESTO and global canopy-height products in the Danum Valley canopy-height task, and substantially improves over SpectralGPT on BioMassters in low-label biomass estimation. The paper also appropriately acknowledges that a task-specific fully supervised BioMassters winner still performs better when all labels are available.

The appendix provides many useful implementation details, including input bands, sequence length, model size, optimizer, batch size, training compute, temporal sampling, loss definition, and downstream-head protocols. This supports reproducibility more than is typical for large-scale EO model submissions.
weaknesses: The empirical comparisons are not uniformly fair or equally strong. Some baselines are static global products while TESSERA is paired with locally trained heads, especially in canopy height and stocking-index experiments. These comparisons are useful operationally, but they do not always isolate representation quality from downstream supervision, local calibration, or product/task mismatch.

The burned-area section is mainly qualitative, relying on UMAP separability over two 15 x 15 km California regions. This supports an interesting diagnostic claim, but not the stronger implication that TESSERA provides a validated scalable burned-area detector. Quantitative metrics against MTBS or a held-out benchmark would be needed for that claim.

Ablations are limited for the main methodological choices. The paper does not clearly quantify the contribution of Sentinel-1 vs Sentinel-2 fusion, temporal sampling, mix-up regularization, projector size, global shuffling, or pretraining scale to downstream performance. This makes it harder to distinguish which parts of TESSERA drive the gains.

Reproducibility still depends on promised releases rather than demonstrated availability in the manuscript. The model, generation code, Rust shuffling pipeline, global representation maps, and exact downstream splits are central to the claimed practical value, but the paper does not provide enough concrete access details or checksums/URLs in the submitted text.

Some presentation and consistency issues weaken confidence. For example, the main figure description refers to GRU pooling while the appendix describes attention pooling; the paper makes broad “state-of-the-art” claims across diverse tasks where the evidence is mixed in strength; and the voluntary-carbon-market section contains placeholders such as “REF” and a typo in “conversion functions.”

The global representation-map claim is ambitious, but storage, access, tiling format, uncertainty, missing-data behavior, and repeated temporal sampling effects are not discussed in enough detail for users to assess operational deployment. These are not fatal flaws, but they matter because accessibility is a central contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem in Earth observation: turning irregular, cloudy, multi-sensor time series into analysis-ready 10 m embeddings. The proposed release of global annual embeddings plus a Python retrieval library is a substantial usability contribution, not just a model architecture contribution.

The system design is sensible for the domain: separate Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 temporal encoders, day-of-year encoding, sparse temporal sampling, cloud/missing-data handling, Barlow Twins-style redundancy reduction, and 8-bit quantized 128D outputs all align with the stated goal of scalable, reusable pixel-level representations.

The empirical scope is broad. The manuscript evaluates crop classification, canopy height, above-ground biomass, burned-area structure, and carbon-market stocking indices, and includes comparisons to PRESTO, Google Satellite Embeddings, SpectralGPT, raw Sentinel composites, random forests, and several operational remote-sensing products.

The strongest evaluations are the crop classification and biomass experiments, where the paper reports label-efficiency trends and uses relevant foundation-model baselines under similar downstream heads. The ablation study also provides useful evidence that global shuffling, mixup regularization, Sentinel-1 fusion, and quantization affect representation quality as claimed.

The work is unusually strong on practical reproducibility for a large EO model: it describes preprocessing, training hyperparameters, model size, compute, downstream heads, data sources, and states that weights, code, embeddings, and tools are released. This is valuable even though reproducing pretraining is expensive.
weaknesses: The main technical novelty is moderate. The architecture and objective are largely a careful domain adaptation of known components: Transformer temporal encoders, Barlow Twins, mixup regularization, modality fusion, and quantization. The contribution is more in scale, engineering, and released data products than in a fundamentally new CV method.

Some headline claims are stronger than the evidence supports. The paper repeatedly claims state-of-the-art or unprecedented accuracy, but several evaluations are narrow or not benchmark-style: canopy height is tested on a single 5 x 6 km Borneo area, burned-area detection is mainly qualitative UMAP analysis over two regions, and the stocking-index experiment uses only 38 private plots from one region.

Baseline fairness is uneven across tasks. For canopy height, TESSERA is locally trained against airborne LiDAR while several global products are used without local calibration, so the comparison demonstrates local adaptability more than direct superiority over those products. For AGB, the authors note that inputs and preprocessing differ from SpectralGPT/BioMassters baselines, complicating interpretation. For patch segmentation, some models appear fine-tuned while TESSERA/GSE/PRESTO are used through different embedding workflows, which may confound architecture, data, and head effects.

The burned-area section is weak as evidence for the claimed capability. It relies primarily on visual UMAP separability and only two randomly selected California regions; there is no robust quantitative detection benchmark across fires, ecosystems, years, cloud regimes, or severity classes. This should be treated as a qualitative case study, not strong validation.

The geographic and temporal generalization evidence is incomplete. Several tasks are single-country or single-region, and the ablation/scaling analysis is tied to Austrian crop classification. Given the model is positioned as global and broadly useful, more held-out continents, years, biomes, and acquisition conditions would be needed to fully substantiate the broadest claims.

There are reproducibility limitations despite the open-source posture. The global embedding product is about 250 TB per year, pretraining requires roughly 6200 GPU hours, and one downstream dataset for stocking indices requires a Data Transfer Agreement. These are understandable at this scale, but they limit independent verification of the largest claims.

Presentation and consistency issues reduce confidence in places. The manuscript alternates between attention pooling and GRU pooling descriptions, the burn-area years differ between the main text and appendix, some figure captions carry most of the numerical evidence instead of tables, and several performance claims lack exact numeric values in the text. These are fixable, but they matter for reviewing technical evidence.

The paper would benefit from a more restrained framing. The contribution is clearly useful and likely impactful, but phrases such as “transformative,” “unprecedented,” and broad “state-of-the-art” claims overreach relative to the mixed strength of the evaluations. A clearer separation between demonstrated results, qualitative case studies, and intended applications would make the scientific case stronger.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and practical problem: making Sentinel-1/2 time-series information usable through precomputed, global, 10 m, annual embeddings. The “embeddings-as-data” framing, the GEOTESSERA library, released model/code, and planned large-scale data products could be useful to many EO practitioners if maintained.

The system is technically plausible and reasonably described: dual Sentinel-1/Sentinel-2 temporal encoders, day-of-year encoding, Barlow Twins-style self-supervision, mixup regularization, quantization-aware embeddings, and global shuffling are all sensible design choices for this domain.
The scale is notable. Pretraining on roughly 800M d-pixels from over 3000 MGRS tiles and producing 128-dimensional int8 global embeddings is a substantial engineering contribution.

The paper evaluates across several downstream applications, including crop classification, canopy height, biomass, fire disturbance visualization, and a carbon-market stocking-index use case, rather than relying on only one benchmark.
The appendices provide many useful implementation details, including architecture size, training hyperparameters, ablations, downstream heads, data splits for some tasks, and availability statements.
weaknesses: The main methodological contribution is limited. The model is largely a domain-scaled combination of known components: transformer time-series encoders, Barlow Twins redundancy reduction, mixup, modality fusion, and precomputed embeddings. The most distinctive contribution is the data product/system, but the paper repeatedly frames this as a state-of-the-art foundation-model advance without a correspondingly novel learning method.

The empirical evidence is uneven and often not strong enough for the breadth of the claims. Some tasks are rigorous enough to be informative, but others are closer to demonstrations. The burned-area section uses only two randomly selected California regions and mainly UMAP separability, with no strong quantitative benchmark against established burned-area methods. This is insufficient to support broad claims about fire detection, timing, or severity mapping.

Several comparisons are not fully controlled. In AGB, TESSERA+UNet is compared to SpectralGPT+UPerNet using different preprocessing and inputs, and to the BioMassters winner under different training/retraining conditions. In canopy height, learned local models are compared against static global products, which the paper itself notes are disadvantaged in local evaluations. These comparisons may be useful context, but they do not cleanly establish representation superiority.

The “state-of-the-art” language is overextended. Many reported gains are shown primarily in plots rather than detailed tables, and some baselines are mismatched in input modality, spatial/temporal coverage, model head, or training protocol. The paper would be stronger if it separated “outperforms under this specific pipeline” from broader SOTA claims.

The evaluation breadth is geographically narrower than the global claims imply. Crop classification is Austria, canopy height is one 5 x 6 km Borneo region, burned area is two California tiles, AGB is BioMassters/Finnish forests, and the stocking-index analysis uses 38 plots in Para. This is valuable diversity, but not enough to validate global generality across ecosystems, latitudes, cloud regimes, sensor coverage, and land-cover types.

The stocking-index experiment has serious evidentiary limitations: only 38 private in-situ plots, rescaling each product to match the field data before comparison, and training the TESSERA-derived index using GEDI relative heights from the same regional context. The resulting R2/RMSE comparison is suggestive but not a robust validation of carbon-market applicability.

The ablation study is narrow: it uses a 100x-downsampled Austrian crop task only. It supports the importance of global shuffling and mixup for that setting, but does not establish that the same components matter for canopy structure, biomass, fire disturbance, or other global downstream tasks.

Reproducibility remains only partial despite the open-source claim. The global embedding map is about 250 TB, some data are private under DTA, training requires around 6200 GPU hours, and some central comparisons depend on large external products and preprocessing pipelines. The paper provides many details, but independent reproduction of the core claims would be difficult.

There are technical/presentation inconsistencies that reduce confidence. For example, the main text/figure description alternates between attention pooling and GRU pooling, the crop figure panel ordering appears inconsistent between text and caption, and several key details are referred to as supplemental or reference [1] rather than being cleanly reported in the main evidence flow.

Overall, the work has real practical value as an EO resource, but the scientific case is not yet convincing enough for acceptance at CVPR: the novelty is mostly systems/data release, the claims are overstated, and several evaluations are insufficiently controlled or too demonstration-like to support the paper’s conclusions.

strengths: Strong practical contribution: TESSERA provides analysis-ready, global, annual, 10 m pixel embeddings from Sentinel-1/2 time series, which is a meaningful usability advance over models that require users to run heavy preprocessing and inference pipelines.

The model design is sensible for Earth observation: modality-specific temporal encoders, day-of-year information, temporal sampling for cloud/missing-data robustness, Barlow Twins-style redundancy reduction, global shuffling, and quantization-aware training all address real EO constraints.

The empirical evaluation is broad and application-relevant, covering crop classification, canopy height, above-ground biomass, burned-area representation, and carbon-market stocking indices. The crop and canopy/biomass experiments especially support the claim that the embeddings are useful with lightweight downstream heads and limited labels.

The paper includes useful ablations and scaling studies. The ablation table shows clear effects of global shuffling and mixup, a moderate contribution from Sentinel-1, and negligible degradation from int8 quantization, which supports the engineering choices behind the data product.

Openness and reproducibility are better than typical large-scale foundation-model submissions: the authors state that model parameters, retrieval/inference/training code, GEOTESSERA tooling, and a 2024 embedding map are available, and most downstream datasets are public.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is moderate. The architecture combines known components, including temporal Transformers, Barlow Twins, mixup-style regularization, and modality fusion; the main novelty is the scale, productization, and EO-specific engineering rather than a fundamentally new learning algorithm.

Several headline claims are stronger than the evidence warrants. The burned-area task is mainly a qualitative UMAP analysis on two California tiles, not a quantitative benchmark against burn mapping methods, so it should not be weighed equally with the crop, canopy, and AGB evaluations.

Evaluation breadth is good, but geographic and temporal coverage of some tasks is narrow: canopy height is a 5 x 6 km Borneo site, stocking indices use 38 private plots in one Brazilian region, and the crop benchmark is Austria. This leaves uncertainty about transfer to other biomes, crop systems, years, and management regimes.

Some baseline comparisons are imperfect. The AGB comparison notes differing input data and unavailable SpectralGPT preprocessing; patch-based models are fine-tuned differently from pixel-embedding models in the segmentation experiment; and global canopy products are compared in a local calibration setting where they are expected to be disadvantaged.

Reproducibility remains challenging despite code/data release claims because pretraining requires about 6200 GPU hours, the embedding product is roughly 250 TB per year, and one downstream task depends on plot data available only under a data transfer agreement.

The paper sometimes overstates causality, for example attributing the stocking-index advantage specifically to TESSERA embedding efficiency despite the use of a trained RF target derived from GEDI and region-specific rescaling. More cautious wording would better match the evidence.
